slides.title: Linear, step and cubic
slides.source: Source: Chapter 10, “Between keys: interpolation, easing, update mode”; glossary, Animation.
slides.notes: Linear and step (UPDATE_DISCRETE) are explained in Chapter 10 "Between keys". Cubic is only listed there, so it is tagged editor or docs, citing the Godot animation introduction page the chapter links. Cubic here is a Catmull-Rom spline computed in code; Godot may use a different cubic, and this is shown as the idea, not as Godot internals.
slides.picture: A plot of four keys. A straight-line curve, a staircase curve and a smooth curve are added one at a time, each with a dot travelling along it and the computed value underneath.

slides.title: Easing from first principles
slides.source: Source: Chapter 10, “Between keys”; glossary, Animation (Easing); Riot ep 6 (ease, spacing).
slides.notes: Formulas: ease-in p = t squared; ease-out p = 1 - (1-t) squared; ease-in-out p = 3t squared - 2t cubed. Speeds are the numerical derivative. Ease-in-out has no glossary row; it is a standard name (CSS and Godot ease curves). Chapter 10 explains the per-key transition value, where 1 is linear.
slides.picture: A curve of progress against time with a dot travelling along it. Beside it, two tracks show where an object is at ten equal time steps: evenly spaced for linear, bunched where the curve is flat for eased.

slides.title: Follow-through, overlap and secondary motion
slides.source: Source: The Illusion of Life, Thomas and Johnston: the 12 principles; named in; Riot series ep 6 Character Animation.
slides.notes: Follow-through, overlap and secondary motion are from the 12 principles the Riot video names but does not teach; tagged outside source. Tail: a damped spring (omega 14, damping ratio 0.22) integrated at 60 fps; hair: follow-the-leader chain with fixed segment length. Both precomputed at load.

slides.title: Rig, rest pose and skinning weights
slides.source: Source: Chapter 10, “Skeletons and IK”; glossary, Animation (Rig, Bone, Skinning weights).
slides.notes: Skeleton, bone, rest pose and weights: Chapter 10 "Skeletons and IK" (Skeleton2D, painted weights, rest pose). Rig is a glossary row. Linear blend skinning is computed per vertex: position = (1 - w) × upper-bone position + w × forearm-bone position, with w a smoothstep across 140 px at the elbow.
slides.picture: Step 1: two bones and a joint bend as a chain. Step 2: a mesh bound rigidly to the bones, with a gap at the elbow when it bends. Step 3: the same mesh with smooth weights, shaded by how much each vertex follows the forearm.

slides.title: FK, IK and retargeting
slides.source: Source: Chapter 10, “Skeletons and IK”; glossary, Animation (FK / IK) and Animation foundations (Retargeting).
slides.notes: IK is explained in Chapter 10 (Skeletons and IK; the Unity two-bone IK passage says the tip of a limb reaches a target). FK and retargeting are glossary only. Two-bone IK uses the law of cosines: cos(elbow) = (d squared - L1 squared - L2 squared) / (2 L1 L2). Retargeting here scales the target by the ratio of total reach.
slides.picture: Step 1: a two-bone arm swings from the shoulder and the hand traces an arc. Step 2: a target moves and the arm solves its angles with the law of cosines, until the target is out of reach. Step 3: one clip on two skeletons, copied angles versus retargeted by IK.

slides.title: Root motion, blend tree and state machine
slides.source: Source: Chapter 11, “Root motion”, “BlendSpace”, “The state machine, as machinery”; glossary, Animation (Root motion, In-place, Blend tree, State machine, Transition, Parameter); Riot series ep 6 Character Animation.
slides.notes: Root motion: Chapter 11 "Root motion". Blend tree and state machine: Chapter 11 "The blend-tree nodes you will use" and "The state machine, as machinery". Transitions and parameters are shown inside the state machine step. Stride 120 px per cycle and code speed 150 px/s are illustrative; the foot slide is their difference. Walk, run amplitudes are illustrative.
slides.picture: Step 1: a walker moved by the clip's root track. Step 2: the same clip in place with code moving it at a different speed. Step 3: a speed parameter sets weights on idle, walk and run clips. Step 4: states with transitions fired by conditions.

new_texts: The clip moves the character through the world.
ROOT MOTION: THE CLIP'S ROOT TRACK TRAVELS
after 4.0 s the root is at x = 480 px
Root motion: the clip's own travel moves the character, so each foot stays put on the ground.
all_texts: The clip moves the character through the world.
ROOT MOTION: THE CLIP'S ROOT TRACK TRAVELS
after 4.0 s the root is at x = 480 px
Root motion: the clip's own travel moves the character, so each foot stays put on the ground.

new_texts: The clip stays on the spot; code does the travel.
SAME WALK CLIP, TWO WAYS TO TRAVEL
root motion: clip moves it, 120 px/s
foot slide: 30 px/s, since one stride covers 120 px but code moves 150
In-place: the clip stays on the spot. If code's speed differs from the stride, the feet slide.

slides.title: Before you ship an animation
slides.source: Source: Chapter 10, “Frames, sprite sheets and cycles”; Chapter 11, “Root motion”; Riot series ep 6 Character Animation.
slides.picture: A checklist of six items drawn one at a time.

new_texts: Do the key poses tell the story, and does each read as a clear silhouette?
Which interpolation sits between the keys: linear, step or cubic?
Does the easing match the weight: gentle starts for heavy things, soft stops?
Do timing and spacing hold at the frame rate and speed scale you will play at?
Does the loop close, with the last key equal to the first and no seam?
Who moves the body, root motion or code, and do the weights bend the mesh cleanly?
Then say it exactly: not “make it smoother”, but “ease-in-out over 0.4 s”.
